text: Milk nourishes the newborn calf. Deep within the udder, glandular tissue contains millions of microscopic sacs called alveoli (about 1 million alveoli per 15 cm³ of udder tissue). Each alveolus is lined with milk-producing cells that draw nutrients from the blood to synthesize lipid, protein, and lactose, while some milk components (vitamins, minerals) are simply filtered from the blood into the milk without synthesis. A large blood supply serves the udder — around 400 liters of blood pass through it to produce a single liter of milk. Muscle cells around each alveolus contract to squeeze milk into the milk ducts; when the calf suckles, this triggers milk let-down, which lasts only about 6 minutes. Between suckling periods, milk accumulates in the alveolar spaces, ducts, and cisterns, and is removed through the teat ducts during milking.
